name: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and biochemical criteria for porphyria cutanea tarda

criteria.description: Elevated urinary uroporphyrins and heptacarboxylporphyrins with characteristic predominance of uroporphyrin
Elevated plasma porphyrins with characteristic fluorescence emission peak at ~619 nm
Elevated isocoproporphyrins in feces (pathognomonic for UROD deficiency)
Characteristic skin lesions on sun-exposed areas (blisters, erosions, milia, scarring, hypertrichosis)
Reduced hepatic UROD enzyme activity (<20% of normal)
Presence of susceptibility factors (hepatitis C, alcohol, estrogen, iron overload, HIV)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Characteristic skin findings plus elevated urinary uroporphyrins with isocoproporphyrins in feces. Type II (familial) confirmed by UROD gene mutation.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Type I (sporadic, ~75-80%) has no UROD mutation; Type II (familial, ~20%) has autosomal dominant UROD mutation; Type III (familial, rare) clusters in families without UROD mutation.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Skin fragility and blistering on sun-exposed areas
pathognomonic.notes: Dorsal hands, forearms, face, ears most commonly affected

common.symptomName: Erosions and crusting on dorsal hands

occasional.notes: Can mimic systemic sclerosis; called pseudoscleroderma

rare.notes: Long-term risk, especially with concurrent hepatitis C

laboratory: Markedly elevated urinary uroporphyrins and heptacarboxylporphyrins
Elevated plasma porphyrins with fluorescence peak ~619 nm
Elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (iron overload)
Normal urinary PBG and ALA (unlike acute porphyrias)
imaging: Liver ultrasound may show hepatomegaly or steatosis
MRI liver for iron quantification if iron overload suspected
Hepatic imaging for HCC surveillance in chronic cases
genetic: UROD gene mutation present in Type II (familial) PCT
HFE gene mutations (C282Y, H63D) common as susceptibility factors
Autosomal dominant inheritance for Type II
other: Wood's lamp examination of urine shows coral-red fluorescence
Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blister with festooning of dermal papillae
PAS-positive thickening of dermal vessel walls

distinguishingFeatures: VP has both cutaneous and neurovisceral symptoms
VP shows elevated fecal protoporphyrin and coproporphyrin
VP has plasma fluorescence peak at ~626 nm
HCP has elevated fecal coproporphyrin III predominantly
HCP may have acute neurovisceral attacks
Clinically indistinguishable skin lesions but no biochemical abnormalities
EBA has anti-type VII collagen antibodies

redFlags: Coexisting hepatitis C infection requiring treatment coordination
Evidence of hepatic cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma
Severe sclerodermoid changes suggesting advanced disease
references: Frank J, Poblete-Gutierrez P. Porphyria cutanea tarda—when skin meets liver. Best Pract Res Clin Gastroenterol. 2010;24(5):735-45.
Puy H, Gouya L, Deybach JC. Porphyrias. Lancet. 2010;375(9718):924-37.
Balwani M, Desnick RJ. The porphyrias: advances in diagnosis and treatment. Blood. 2012;120(23):4496-504.
Ryan Caballes F, et al. Hepatitis C, porphyria cutanea tarda and liver iron: an update. Liver Int. 2012;32(6):880-93.
